title: Joining Tables Together
subtitle: Foreign keys and JOINs — how two tables become one answer.

lessons.title: Foreign keys — linking two tables
lessons.summary: Why one big table is a bad idea, and how a foreign key ties two tables together.
lessons.examTip: A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. It enforces referential integrity — you cannot record a child row that points at a parent that does not exist.

lines.text: Up to now we have had one table. Students. And it worked perfectly.
Now the college says, we also need to know which courses each student is taking.
Your first instinct will be to add columns. course_one, course_two, course_three.
Please do not. Let me explain why that idea fails.
First, how many columns do you make? What happens when a student takes a fourth course?
Second, if the course name Database Concepts is typed into four thousand student rows, and the college renames the course, you must fix four thousand rows.
Third, somebody will type Database Concepts, somebody else will type Databse Concepts with a spelling mistake, and now your reports are wrong forever.
That repeating of the same information is called data redundancy, and it is the enemy. Learn that phrase.
So we do it the proper way. Each kind of thing gets its own table.
Students in a students table. Courses in a courses table. And then we link them.

steps.title: The parent table
steps.expect: Three courses, each with its own course_id.

lines.text: So first, a table for the courses themselves.
course_id as the primary key, the course name, and the lecturer who teaches it.
And I am putting three courses in. Database Concepts, Programming Concepts, and Computer Networking.
Notice each course is written once. Once, in the whole database.
If the college renames Database Concepts tomorrow, I change one row, and every report in the college is instantly correct.
Run.
Three courses.
Course one, two and three. Remember those numbers, because we are about to use them.

steps.title: The child table and the foreign key
steps.typeCue: Now look at the last line
steps.expect: Four enrolment rows — just numbers, linking students to courses.

lines.text: Now the clever part. We need a third table to record who is doing what.
We call it enrolments. And it holds almost nothing. Just numbers.
Now look at the last line inside the brackets.
FOREIGN KEY, open bracket, course_id, close bracket, REFERENCES courses, open bracket, course_id, close bracket.
Read that in English. The course_id in this table refers to the course_id in the courses table.
That is a foreign key. Say the definition with me.
A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table.
The courses table is the parent. The enrolments table is the child. The child points at the parent.
And now the database will refuse to accept an enrolment for course number nine, because there is no course number nine.
That protection has a name, and it is examinable. Referential integrity. Write it down.
Now look at the rows I am inserting. One and one. One and two. Two and one. Three and three.
Run.
Look at that table.
Just numbers. No names anywhere. And yet all the information is in there.
Student one is doing course one and course two. Student two is doing course one. Student three is doing course three.
Tanaka is doing Databases and Programming. Rudo is doing Databases. Chipo is doing Networking.
But nobody wants to read numbers like that. In the next lesson we turn these numbers back into names.

marks.cue: FOREIGN KEY, open bracket, course_id, close bracket, REFERENCES courses
Now look at the rows I am inserting

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: Three definitions come out of this lesson, and they are worth easy marks.
One. What is a foreign key? A field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, used to link the two tables.
Two. What is referential integrity? A rule ensuring that a foreign key value must always refer to an existing record in the related table.
Three. What is data redundancy? The unnecessary repetition of the same data in a database, which wastes space and can lead to inconsistency.
And a practical question will say, write a statement to create the enrolments table with a foreign key referencing courses.
The line they want to see is FOREIGN KEY, brackets, the column, REFERENCES, the other table, brackets, its primary key.
Learn the shape of that line. FOREIGN KEY here, REFERENCES there.

lessons.title: INNER JOIN — turning numbers back into names
lessons.summary: Reading two tables in one query by matching the key columns.
lessons.examTip: SELECT columns FROM tableA INNER JOIN tableB ON tableA.key = tableB.key; The ON clause says which columns must match. Prefix each column with its table name when both tables have a column of that name.

steps.title: The problem we are solving
steps.typeCue: Look at the enrolments table again
steps.expect: Four rows of pure numbers. Correct data, useless report.

lines.text: I have put our three tables back, exactly as we left them. Students, courses, and enrolments.
Look at the enrolments table again.
Run.
Numbers.
One and one. One and two. Two and one. Three and three.
The data is perfect. But if I print this and put it on the notice board, nobody knows what it means.
The names are in the students table. The course names are in the courses table. And the link is here.
So we need a way to read all three tables in one question. That is a JOIN.

steps.title: Your first JOIN
steps.sql:
SELECT students.first_name, students.surname, enrolments.course_id
FROM students
INNER JOIN enrolments
  ON students.student_id = enrolments.student_id;
steps.expect: Names next to course numbers — half the job done.

lines.text: Let us start with two tables only, students and enrolments, and add the third one afterwards.
Watch these four lines carefully. This is the shape of every join you will ever write.
Line one. SELECT, and the columns I want. And look how I write them.
students dot first_name. enrolments dot course_id. Table name, dot, column name.
Why the dot? Because both tables have a column called student_id, and the database must know which one you mean.
Line two. FROM students. That is my first table.
Line three. INNER JOIN enrolments. That is my second table.
Line four, and this is the heart of it. ON students dot student_id equals enrolments dot student_id.
The ON clause is the matching rule. It says, a row from here belongs with a row from there when these two numbers are the same.
That is the whole idea of a join. Find the rows that match, and put them side by side.
Run.
Now look at that.
Tanaka appears twice, with course one and course two, because he is doing two courses.
Rudo has course one. Chipo has course three.
The names came from one table, the course numbers came from another, and they arrived in one answer.
And notice Blessing is not there at all. She is not enrolled in anything, so there was nothing to match her with.
Remember that. INNER JOIN only shows rows that have a match on both sides.

marks.cue: students dot first_name. enrolments dot course_id
ON students dot student_id equals enrolments dot student_id

steps.title: Joining three tables
steps.sql:
SELECT students.first_name, students.surname, courses.course_name, courses.lecturer
FROM students
INNER JOIN enrolments
  ON students.student_id = enrolments.student_id
INNER JOIN courses
  ON enrolments.course_id = courses.course_id;
steps.typeCue: So I add two more lines
steps.expect: A proper report — names, course names and lecturers, all in words.

lines.text: We are half way. We have names and course numbers. Now let us turn those numbers into course names.
The course names live in the courses table, so we join that one on as well.
So I add two more lines. Another INNER JOIN, and another ON.
INNER JOIN courses, ON enrolments dot course_id equals courses dot course_id.
And now in the SELECT line I can ask for courses dot course_name and courses dot lecturer.
See the chain? Students link to enrolments. Enrolments link to courses.
The enrolments table is the bridge in the middle. It touches both sides.
That middle table has a name in the exam. It is called a junction table, or a link table.
Run.
Now that. That is a report.
Tanaka Moyo, Database Concepts, Mr Chirwa.
Tanaka Moyo, Programming Concepts, Ms Sibanda.
Rudo Ncube, Database Concepts. Chipo Banda, Computer Networking.
Not one number on the screen. Every single thing is in words, and the principal can read it.
And remember, that came out of three separate tables that each store their information only once.
That is what a relational database is. That is the whole reason it is called relational.

marks.cue: INNER JOIN courses, ON enrolments dot course_id equals courses dot course_id
courses dot course_name and courses dot lecturer

steps.title: Short names for long queries
steps.sql:
SELECT s.first_name, s.surname, c.course_name
FROM students s
INNER JOIN enrolments e
  ON s.student_id = e.student_id
INNER JOIN courses c
  ON e.course_id = c.course_id
ORDER BY s.surname;
steps.expect: Exactly the same report, sorted by surname, written in half the space.

lines.text: That last query was correct, but look how long it was. students dot this, enrolments dot that, over and over.
So we give each table a short nickname, just for this query.
Look at the FROM line.
FROM students s. Just a letter after the table name. That s now means students for the rest of the query.
INNER JOIN enrolments e. INNER JOIN courses c.
And now everywhere I write s dot first_name, c dot course_name. Much shorter, much easier to read.
This is the same alias idea we met with AS in Chapter Four, but for tables instead of columns.
You can also write FROM students AS s, with the word AS. Both are correct.
And I have added ORDER BY at the bottom, to sort it by surname, because a join is still just a SELECT.
Run.
Exactly the same report, sorted alphabetically.
Banda, Moyo, Moyo, Ncube. Same data, half the typing.
In the exam, use aliases the moment you join three tables. It saves time and it saves mistakes.

marks.cue: FROM students s. Just a letter after the table name
INNER JOIN enrolments e. INNER JOIN courses c
And I have added ORDER BY at the bottom

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: Join questions carry big marks, and they are also where students freeze. So let me give you a recipe.
Step one. Read the question and write down which pieces of information they want.
Step two. For each piece, write down which table it lives in. Name, students. Course name, courses.
Step three. Ask, is there a table in the middle that links them? Usually yes.
Step four. Write FROM the first table, then INNER JOIN each other table, each one with its own ON.
Step five. Every ON is always primary key equals foreign key. Every single time.
Primary key equals foreign key. If you remember nothing else about joins, remember that.
And the definition question. What is a join? A join combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them.
One more warning. If you forget the ON clause completely, you do not get an error. You get every row matched with every row.
Four students times four enrolments is sixteen rows of nonsense. That is called a Cartesian product, and it is worth knowing the name.

items.cue: Every ON is always primary key equals foreign key
items.text: Every ON is primary key = foreign key.   Every single time.
A join combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them.

items.cue: if you forget the ON clause completely
items.text: No ON clause = every row matched with every row. That is a Cartesian product — know the name.

lessons.title: LEFT JOIN — including the ones with nothing
lessons.summary: When the rows that are missing are the ones you actually need to find.
lessons.examTip: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, and NULL where the right table has no match.

steps.title: Who did the INNER JOIN hide?
steps.sql:
SELECT s.first_name, s.surname, e.course_id
FROM students s
INNER JOIN enrolments e
  ON s.student_id = e.student_id;
steps.expect: Four rows — and Blessing Sibanda is nowhere to be seen.

lines.text: In the last lesson I said something quickly, and now I want to slow down on it, because it matters.
I said Blessing was not in our results, because she is not enrolled in anything.
Run our inner join again and look for her.
Run it.
Tanaka twice, Rudo, Chipo.
No Blessing. She has vanished from the report.
Now think about that from the college's point of view.
Blessing is the one student who has registered but has not chosen any courses.
She is the exact person the registrar needs to phone. And our report is hiding her.
The INNER JOIN threw her away, because she had no match on the other side.
So sometimes the rows that are missing are the most important rows of all.

steps.title: LEFT JOIN keeps everybody
steps.sql:
SELECT s.first_name, s.surname, e.course_id
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrolments e
  ON s.student_id = e.student_id;
steps.expect: Five rows now — Blessing appears, with an empty course_id.

lines.text: So we change one word. One single word.
One word changes. INNER becomes LEFT.
LEFT JOIN. Everything else in the query stays exactly the same.
And here is what LEFT means. The left table is the one in the FROM line. In our case, students.
LEFT JOIN says, give me every row from the left table, no matter what.
If there is a match on the right, show it. If there is no match, show NULL.
Run.
There she is.
Blessing Sibanda, and her course_id is empty. That empty space is NULL.
Nobody was thrown away this time. All four students are accounted for.
And that NULL is not a mistake. That NULL is the answer. It is telling us she has no enrolment.

marks.cue: One word changes. INNER becomes LEFT

steps.title: Using the NULL to find the gaps
steps.sql:
SELECT s.first_name, s.surname
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrolments e
  ON s.student_id = e.student_id
WHERE e.course_id IS NULL;
steps.expect: Just Blessing — the exact list the registrar asked for.

lines.text: Now we finish the job properly.
The registrar did not ask for all the students. She asked for the ones with no courses.
And we know that those students, and only those students, have a NULL in the course column.
So we add a WHERE, using what we learned in Chapter Four.
WHERE e dot course_id IS NULL.
And remember the rule from that lesson. Never equals NULL. Always IS NULL.
Run.
One row. Blessing Sibanda.
That is the phone list. One name, and it is exactly the right name.
Look at what you just did. You used a LEFT JOIN to find something that is not there.
Students with no courses. Courses with no students. Customers who have never ordered.
That pattern, LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL, is one of the most useful things in this whole course. Keep it.

marks.cue: WHERE e dot course_id IS NULL

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: The exam asks this one directly. Distinguish between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN.
INNER JOIN returns only the records that have matching values in both tables.
LEFT JOIN returns all the records from the left table, together with the matching records from the right table. Where there is no match, NULL is returned.
Two sentences. Learn them as they are.
You should also be able to name the others, even if you never use them.
RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image. All the rows from the right table.
And FULL OUTER JOIN keeps everything from both sides. MySQL does not support it directly, and that itself is sometimes a question.
But when a question uses the words all students, including those who, or even if they have none, that is your signal.
Those words mean LEFT JOIN. Every time.
